excerpt:
Spring rolls
Roti with peanut sauce
Popcorn chicken
Pork dumplings

It was busy in the Vietnamese Restaurant and Cafe on this Saturday afternoon.  But they were clearly used to it, because our food came fast, they cleared tables fast, we watched in awe as their well oiled machine just turned over and turned over.

We’d be happy to eat everything again, except for the dumplings, which were too dumpy, and not lingy enough. Honestly they were pretty much just a ball of pork that was encased, they weren’t awful, but the innards just didn’t have a nice texture. The roti was really good, fantastically hot and fresh, crispy, with great laminations, not greasy, chef’s kiss.The popcorn chicken had an artisanal flair, nice and small but irregular in size and had a tasty dipping sauce and welcome side of peanuts. Even the salad actually was helpful to cut through the greasiness. Lastly, the spring rolls were also great. They were absolutely burning hot, so do be careful, but they had a varied filling that was very welcome and their sweet chilli sauce was thick for dipping which we appreciated.

title: Advieh Restaurant and Bar
excerpt:
Lamb dumpings
Carrots
Chips
Pide
Lamb neck with flatbread

Advieh serves Middle Eastern food with sophistication and flair. We loved everything. Even the chips were exceptional - super thick, hand cut, crispy, piping hot, perfectly seasoned, some kind of creamy dipping sauce, sweet heaven it was ecstasy. The dumplings were well structured and flavourful, the lamb neck absolutely falling off the bone. Every single dish was perfectly cooked and exciting.

Sounds like a 4 huh?

It would have been if not for the abysmal service. They didn’t take our order, not even a drinks order, we had to flag a guy down who had been working at a computer literally next to us, who then complained to us that we weren’t in his section. They never offered us a second round of drinks, or even refilled our water until right as we were about to leave. They forgot two of the items we ordered, and then had the gall to lie to us, saying they totally hadn’t forgotten them and just had to make more pide dough. Sorry, do you expect us to believe you made a fresh batch of yeasted dough in this time? Pull the other one mate. And to add insult to injury they never bothered to clear a single one of our plates. It’s not like they were rushed off their feet either, we were late diners and they had plenty of time to set the empty tables all around us. For shame sir, for shame.

title: Ki Maha Restaurant Waiheke Island
excerpt:
Goat cheese fritters
Duck croquettes
Olive flatbread

ki maha has lovely staff. We made Ki Maha home for a couple of hours, sipping cocktails and nibbling snacks, straddling the lunch to dinner shifts which meant we had two servers. Both were attentive, but not hovery, friendly but not overbearing, and decidedly chill.

All the food was delish, although what is the definition of a fritter? This was a fried ball of goats cheese and decidedly less flat than we were anticipating. They were also $8 each for a golf ball size, which is pretty steep. But hot damn was it good. Paired with a spicy honey we were absolutely loving it. We were also loving the flatbread which was insanely flavourful, hot, crispy, and just the right amount of oily. The least strong was the duck croquettes, which were perfectly good but didn’t blow us away.

title: Vino Vino Restaurant & Bar
excerpt:
Beef burger with coleslaw and chips
Eye fillet with chimichurri, roast potatoes, salad and portobello mushroom

Vino vino serves European fare with some South American influences. the eye fillet was a very nice piece of meat, well cooked, and the mushroom went well. The chimichurri was a non-event, a sprinkle of some green stuff which you could see but not taste, it may as well not have been there. The salad was a time-waste and the potatoes were nice but more like wedges than roast, and there weren’t many to boot.

The steak was a triumph compared to the burger. The patty was remarkable in its dryness and how little it tasted of anything. Definitely no south American flair here. We couldn’t even detect a sauce, there was no cheese, there was certainly no bacon or onion ring or anything exciting. Just a dry patty, two over-crisp buns and a sad pile of salad. The accompanying coleslaw had no flavour, but at least the chips were okay.

title: Tirohana Estate
excerpt:
Pear, walnut and blue cheese tart
Zucchini fritters
Lamb pot pie with mash and roast vegetables
Stuffed chicken breast with roast vegetables
Pumpkin bread and butter pudding with caramel sauce and ice cream
White chocolate berry cheesecake

If you’re looking for a fancy dining experience on a budget, look no further than Tirohana Estate. Shout out to the $72pp dinner which was three generously sized courses, plus an opening drink, amous bouche and petit fours. Definitely good value, and the food wasn’t bad at all. Nor was it perfect - the tart wasn’t very flavourful, the lamb in the pie was chewy and there were some corners of the chicken breast that were laughably dry. But then again the zucchini fritters were fun, the flavour of both mains very enjoyable, and that bread and butter pudding was downright delicious.

Tirohana Estate had friendly, genuine and attentive service. In an unusual move, the waitress read us basically the whole menu. We appreciate when a server points out menu areas of interest or importance e.g. the fish of the day is gurnard, the lamb is meant to be shared for two, we are out of the ratatouille. But this recital went on and on with no apparent point. We were also served two of the worst espresso martinis we have had in a long time. We’re pretty sure it wasn’t shaken, it had no head on it which made the three garnish coffee beans look very silly, it certainly had no actual espresso in it and I’m not sure it even had cold press. I’d wager we were looking at way too much kahlua, some vodka and a bit of simple syrup, swirled around then plonked into a cheap looking over-fat stemmed martini glass. That’s a no from us, just stick to the wine.

title: Pho Nem Hanoi Home Cooking
excerpt:
Vegetable spring rolls
Pork spring rolls
Chicken with ginger rice and coleslaw
Caramelised pork belly with rice and coleslaw

Before we tear Pho Nem a new one, we’ll point out that we suspect we got a below average showing from the Hanoi Home Cooks tonight. Business Andy’s mum comes here every week, and this place was packed, so we don’t reckon they could be stuffing up this hard every night. However, we can only judge the experience that we had. And the experience that we had sucked.

Talk about wait times! We waited about 40 minutes just to get our order taken, and who knows how much longer it would have been if we hadn’t gone up to the counter to beg somebody to come and attend to us. The waiter was friendly but seemed thoroughly frazzled, as though his colleague hadn’t shown up for work and he couldn’t believe he was having to try and do all of this alone.

The spring rolls were both enjoyable, but unfortunately the mains were both sub par. The chicken had the unwelcome surprise of being on the bone. And with only chopsticks and a spoon provided to try and pull dry fried chicken off the bone? Forget about it, you’ve no choice but to eat it KFC style. We will give credit to the ginger rice though, which was the best part of the meal.

What does the word caramelised mean to you? For us it conjured images of crispy pork belly where the corners have some kind of sugar dressing that’s gone crisp and sticky. Boy were we wrong. Blubbery bits of pork belly in a nondescript brown soup where the meat was dry and the fat was smudgey. This thing was foul. The Fee-Rex had one bite and was like hell no. Business Andy, in a fit of politeness and mummys-boy-ism had said that he liked it, so ended up eating most of the meal. Sucker.

Bookings recommended

title: Craggy Range
excerpt:
Bread with apple cider butter and honey
Raw lamb and beetroot tart
Confit duck pastry
Roast halloumi
Stuffed quail and potato
Leek and onion tart
Venison rack with black pudding
Brussel sprouts with roasted nuts
Garlic roast potatoes
Chocolate truffles

Sweet heavens Craggy range does nice food. We won’t spend too much time labouring each individual dish. There were a lot of them, the menu changes monthly, but it was 10s across the board. Particular shout out to the halloumi which was a chunky roasted block, which was a new and welcome way of enjoying this cheese for us. Oh and the bread, so soft yet with such a crunchy crust, the butter was really different, this kind of bread makes you wonder if you should be making bread at home, until you realise it would never taste like this.

While the meal was expensive, it was absolutely in line with the quality, and the servings were very generous. We weren’t chungus after this meal, but we certainly didn’t need any more food. In the spirit of nitpicking, the head on the espresso martinis was over-large, and the vodka espresso martini was too sweet. This was no dampener on what was an excellent dining experience.

Bookings recommended.

title: The Horseman's Cafe
excerpt:
Banana smoothie
Macchiato (?)
Chicken and spinach filo
Stuffed kumara
Citrus tart
Melting moment

Horseman cafe is a Shannon institution, with The Fee-Rex remembering visiting 15 years ago. They continue to be popular, running a steady Sunday lunch trade which the kitchen seemed to be struggling with. “It’ll be 20 minutes for cooked food” they said. While we don’t mind a time warning, actually we appreciate it and adjusted our order accordingly, her tone was clear: “Don’t order any cooked food, I’m overwhelmed”.

Our cabinet fare came out erratically. We were given the biscuit at the counter. Pause. Next came the two heated savoury items. Pause. Later came a matcha. Yes, a matcha, not the macchiato we had ordered. More pause. Out comes the banana smoothie, and we finally question where our tart ended up. Turns out it had been forgotten, but does show up less than a minute after we enquired.

The only thing worth eating was the melting moment. It wasn’t groundbreaking, we’ve absolutely had better, but it was alright and we wouldn’t be sad to eat it again. The filo wasn’t overly enjoyable, the spinach was a bit fibrous, the capsicum chutney inside was over-sweet and the beetroot relish wasn’t a great accompaniment. The filo was a meh.

The other three things we ordered (and we’re not including the random matcha in this) were all bad. The stuffed kumara contained huge chunks of unmashed boiled kumara, the other contents were nondescript, and you had to seriously ration the paltry blobs of sour cream provided.

This was our first banana smoothie in a while, and it was a sad return for this BAATFR classic. The most obvious flaw was that this this beverage did not appear to contain any actual banana, which in our book means it does not meet the definition of a banana smoothie at all. There were sickly slicks of banana syrup decoratively cascaded down the inside of the cheap plastic cup. Bros, come on. We’re not huge fans of that technique at the best of times when honey is used, as it doesn’t actually add anything to the flavour of the drink. Doing this with your cheap nasty banana syrup is just offensive. Speaking of offensive, put your smoothie in a glass you lazy monkeys! This drink was served in one of those compostable “plastic” takeaway cold drink containers, sans straw. Out of a glass we don’t mind no straw, but today this was a problem because 1) you had to deal with the lip feel of this naff plastic, and 2) this thing was a foamy baby. The first mouthful was just bubbles, and the next few weren’t much better. As a final insult, she hadn’t even passed the temperature test, the whole thing was a tepid mess.

Finally we had the citrus tart. This looked alright in the cabinet, and a nice citrus tart is one of the world’s finest things. They’d even made their own pastry. Unfortunately, the pastry was not good at all. It was too thick and had a rubbery, cardboardy texture. They would have been better off purchasing a pre-made tart casing, at least then it would have been crisp. Lemon curd within a citrus tart should be citrusy and tart - it’s in the name! This was lacking in both departments, with the desired tang being replaced with a glum, sweet, lemon-adjacent goop.

The nicest thing we can say about The Horseman’s Cafe was that they had Country Life magazines available for customers. This is something different, and what a great read. As of 2025 there was a Scottish castle for sale, 20 bedroom, accessible only by ferry, and boy was it a fixer upper. But it was only 750,000 quid! Maybe we’ll take the profits from the immense commercial success of this restaurant review site and try our hand at castle restoration. Something to think about…

title: Little Whisky
excerpt:
Fig, feta, and  walnut pizza
Basque cheesecake with cherries and sliced almonds

We really weren’t expecting much from Little Whisky, which is essentially an add on extra thing to Sweet Axe and their upstairs function room, Whisky & Wood. But my god, that pizza. Absolutely fantastic. The cheese was so stringy and cheesy, like those ads you see for Pizza Hutt with the big strings and go “pfft their pizza never strings like that” - this pizza strings like that. Our only complaint is that it came in a box instead of on a board, and had no side plates. Treat us like diners, not students avoiding eating in the rain.

Don’t let our plate complaint imply that the service was inattentive, because it was great. We suspect our server was also the owner, we really liked his chipper mood, he even cut some sick shapes on his way through the room. Unfotunately the cheesecake didn’t quite land. We ordered it because Business Andy loves Basque cheesecakes, in fact he wont shut up about them (do not let him talk about Basque cheesecakes). This one had clearly been made in a big square tin, then cut up into pieces and refrigerated, which kind of ruined the texture, and made it feel a bit too cold. We liked the idea of the cherries and almonds on top, but in the end it was only an okay cheesecake. Nonetheless, we were impressed with Little Whisky’s hustle and think more poeple should visit to enjoy their exceptionally good pizzas.

title: Baobab Cafe
excerpt:
BEEF LASAGNE
PORRIDGE WITH COCONUT YOGHURT AND SEASONAL FRUIT
ORANGE AND ALMOND CAKE

BAOBAB CAFE IS A POPULAR PLACE FOR SUNDAY LUNCH, WITH A GOOD LOOKING CABINET, COOKED OPTIONS THAT STRETCH A BIT BEYOND THE MUNDANE, AND AN OUTDOOR GARDEN TO BOOT. WE ALSO SPOTTED WHAT LOOKED LIKE A COCKTAIL CAPABLE BAR, THEY CERTAINLY HAD THE GLASSWARE, BUT WE DIDN’T SPY AN ALCOHOLIC DRINKS MENU ANYWHERE OR SEE ANYBODY SERVED FROM THE BAR SO NOT QUITE SURE ABOUT THAT ONE.

WHAT’S UP WITH THE ALL CAPS? IT’S A REFLECTION OF HOW LOUD YOU NEED TO TALK IN BAOBAB CAFE. TURN THE DAMN MUSIC DOWN! THEIR JAZZY INSTRUMENTAL JAMS WERE CRANKED TO THE POINT THAT THEY WERE DISTRACTING, ESPECIALLY WHEN ADDED TO THE NOISE OF THE OTHER DINERS. A BIT OF A SHAME, BECAUSE THE FOOD WAS REALLY GOOD ACROSS THE BOARD.

IT SEEMS LIKE PEOPLE REALLY STRUGGLE TO REHEAT A BIG SLAB OF LASAGNA, THIS IS NOT THE FIRST TIME. TO BE FAIR, THIS WAS ONE OF THE BETTER REHEATS THAT WE’VE HAD, BUT IT WAS STILL UNEVEN. WE SURMISE THAT CAFES ARE REALLY STUCK BETWEEN WANTING TO BE FAST AND WANTING TO BE GOOD ON THIS FRONT, WE DON’T KNOW THE SOLUTION, MAYBE CUTTING IT UP BEFORE HEATING IT WOULD BE BETTER? IT WAS LOVELY OTHERWISE. BUT YOU CAN LEAVE THAT SLICE OF TOMATO OFF THE TOP, NOBODY IS EATING THAT AFTER IT’S BEEN BAKED THEN MICROWAVED. WE GET THAT IT ADDS SOME AESTHETIC APPEAL, BUT DON’T SERVE US FOOD YOU DON’T EXPECT US TO EAT. ALSO, STRANGELY THIS LASAGNE CAME WITH A SIDE OF TOMATO SAUCE. title: PhuThai Esarn Restaurant
excerpt:
Khao soi chicken
Tofu pad Thai

When Business Andy came here for a work do a couple of years ago, he wasn’t that impressed. He had a great time, but he also drank far too much soju - perhaps this was a contributing factor. At any rate, two years later PhuThai Esarn Restaurant is still here, and continues to meh.

The Fee-Rex is a sucker for a pad Thai, even though many of them are only so-so, as was the case here. Also massive points off for some of your tofu being cold, a most unwelcome surprise. The khao soi just didn’t have an awful lot going on. There was some chilli oil on the side you could add to spice things up, but this was just bringing heat without doing anything for flavour. While the chicken was of acceptable quality, some crispening would have gone a long way to improving this dish.

We also boldly ordered two cocktails. We don’t normally bother with cocktails when a place only lists a handful of bog standards (pina colada, dark & stormy etc). However, PhuThai had a couple which sounded interesting - one made with Thai milk tea and another a play on a Mai Tai. These were disappointingly poor, and despite their simplicty took forever to make, arriving after our food. Also they contained short straws only 2.5mm longer than the drink, and shorter than the glass once they fell into the stupid divot in the centre. This meant at best you had to fish in with your fingers to get it, at worst it was fully submerged in the Mariana Trench.

title: Newtown Seafood
excerpt:
Two chicken burgers
Battered fish
Battered pineapple ring

The following is a true story. Two days ago , waiting for a bus, we were discussing dine in fish and chips shops and why they weren’t a thing. Today, the first place we saw to eat in Newtown was a dine in fish and chip shop that had just opened. Did we manifest this I to existence,? We see no other plausible explanation.

And thank god that we did, because it was really good. The fish was fresh, the batter, light, it came with a slice of lemon, and had just the right amount of salt on it. Likewise the chicken in the chicken burgers was crispy and delicious, perfectly fried, in fact the entire burger package was just right, fresh lettuce, not too much onion, soft buns. And it was real fried chicken,not a composite chicken smush patty like you might expect. And then the pineapple ring, it was absolutely covered in cinnamon and sugar, had a thick crispy batter, and was miraculously not too hot. We wondered, given how new this place is, whether what we were experiencing was the miraculous benefits of new fryer oil? I guess time will tell whether their quality remains high.

Given this glowing praise, we had to ask ourselves whether this was a 4. We decided it wasn’t, for the following reasons, but they weren’t far off. While the sign said “dine in” they hadn’t really gone to much effort to make that a good experience, it was chilly, there was no cutlery, few serviettes, really the only thing they did was put food on a tray instead of wrapping it up in paper. It really wouldn’t have taken much to make dining in a more pleasant experience. The chicken burger had nailed everything it set out to do, but it was conservative in its ambitions. An interesting sauce, a sneaky hash brown slipped in, or some pickle could all have bumped him closer to the top.

title: Nam Nam Bowen
excerpt:
Tofu bahn mi
Chicken fried rice

Nam nam caters to the business crowd, tired workers who just want to nip out for a bite as close to the office as possible. To that end the service and food delivery were fast, and the effort put into the dishes was acceptable but not more. Both meals were fine, you weren’t angry to eat them, but they hadn’t tried to climb the highest mountain.

The chicken had some pleasant crispness in spots but was pedestrian in flavour and the veg was just frozen veggie mix like your mum would put in a stir fry when she couldn’t be bothered. The banh MI had nice bread and fresh veg but the tofu lacked flavour. And don’t blame that on us ordering tofu, which can be very flavourful when done correctly.

title: Masala Cafe & Bar
excerpt:
Wellington lamb curry
Kadai paneer
Masala special naan
Plain naan

Indian restaurants, real talk. Get somebody to proofread your menus. Even a Microsoft Word spellcheck would have done you a lot of favours here. Although perhaps this is not a negative factor, but rather a marker of authenticity. Speaking of authentic, many restaurants claim to have homemade paneer, but you actually do. Kudos. Likewise the lamb in the mysterious “Wellington” curry was of good quality. The curry sauces themselves were perfectly good, but not exceptional.

What was exceptional was the masala special naan. This is a naan stuffed with chicken and vegetables, cut up like a pizza then served with butter chicken sauce for dipping. And it was killer, easily the best thing of the night. The plain naans definitely couldn’t keep pace, as they were a bit thin and dry.

title: The Beijing Restaurant
excerpt:
Orange beef fried rice
Fried chicken
Fried dumplings

After something off a revamp, there’s some new additions to the menu at the Beijing, some new furniture, and a bit of a new vibe. We are long time Beijing patrons, with it being in our takeaway rotation. It made us nervous when we saw the revamp, which included the edition of a bunch of non-Chinese fried options (fried chicken and fish and chip shop options like nuggets and sausages). Is the Beijing struggling? We suggest the new menu, and the fact that they are generally not very busy when we get our takeaway, implies that they are.

We’re not helping much by not giving them a glowing review, but we can only review what arrived in front of us, and what arrived in front of us had some issues. The dumplings were super oily, were strangely floppy, and didn’t taste particularly good. The fried rice was only average, and the orange beef, while tasty and fresh, was perplexingly piled to one side instead of worked through it. It was like two separate meals and the stressful task of mixing ratios fell to us, the unsuspecting diners. And the fried chicken was just not quite good enough either, its extremities were borderline burnt, and there wasn’t nearly enough of the admittedly nice sweet soy sauce.

title: Penthouse Cinema and Cafe
excerpt:
Mince & cheese pie
Fish & chips
Caramel slice

On a wintery Sunday at lunchtime, Penthouse Cinema & Cafe was absolutely heaving. The cinema tickets and cafe queue is shared and the line was almost out the door. Thanks to the recent release of Toy Story 5 and the latest Minions movie, there were kids everywhere, plus tonnes of senior citizens. The staff were rushed off their feet, but were still friendly and were clearly trying their best amidst difficult circumstances.

Given how busy it was, we thought we might be in for a treat. When the pie was $10, we accepted the price as an indicator of quality. How wrong we were. The pie did appear to be homemade and had good pastry, but what was up with that mince? You remember when you were flatting and you made that stir fry and it was just mince, onion and mixed veg, everybody hated it and you’d made a metric tonne of it? These pie innards were that, but without the veg. Where was the gravy? Where was the cheese? The salt? The pepper? And where was the heat? This thing was tepid at best. When we realised we’d paid $10 for it, we couldn’t help but laugh. And this was not an isolated incident - the man at the table next to us very angrily took his pie up to be reheated, then later, when his reheated pie finally showed up he got up again and told them that he just wanted a refund. This issue is systemic, people.

The fish and chips were better, but it’s hard to be worse. When the fish showed up looking very angular we were worried it was going to be a gross composite hoki fillet. To their credit, it was real fish fillet. To their debit, what was with the crumb? It was so crisp, when you tried to cut into it the shell immediately shattered and completely parted ways with the fish, which also disintegrated. This left you desperately picking little bits up from among the chips, we felt like anteaters trying to get little ants from a rotten log. The salad wasn’t great, why was there cabbage in it? We did at least enjoy the shoestring fries, and both the fries and the fish were hot out of the deep fryer.

The best part was the caramel slice. The portion was generous, the caramel thick, and the edge was extra sticky and delicious, a boon considering often the edge of a slice is often the worst bit.

Bringing us back down to earth; the espresso martinis. Firstly, they didn’t arrive until we were eating our food, which was already a long wait. They had a bitterness which was unpleasant - was the coffee burnt? Perhaps it was the ratios, something to do with the kahlua? Either way, they were bad. They weren’t quite Tirohana Estate bad, but still pretty bad.

title: The Bridge Bar & Restaurant
excerpt:
Cauliflower steak with mash and salad
Korean fried chicken with rice and slaw

On a Friday night at 6:30, The Bridge was doing a steady trade in the 50+ crowd. Perhaps it was the tellies showing 4 different sports simultaneously, perhaps it was the 70s jams with music videos played two seconds out of sync, perhaps it was the tantalising offer of free snacks at 7pm. We were very keen to ensure that we got our share of all - women’s motor racing, the Blues Brothers, and we made damn sure we had purchased a drink between 630 and 7 which gave us the coveted access to grab some fried goodies from the roving grazing platter which went past our table between 7 and 7:05.

Much as we love free fried goods, we paid a hefty price. Perhaps not financially, the monetary cost was actually quite reasonable, but the spiritual cost was heavy. We had three different cocktails and they were all bad. We do give The Bridge a modicum of credit for having a cocktail menu at all, as it was stretching their bounds. But the Tom Collins and Negroni were both awful, and the on-tap espresso martini wasn’t worth having.

Neither was the food. The cauliflower steak was woody as heck and not crispy as advertised. It at least had an interesting spice blend, which is more than you could say about the bland mash. The Korean fried chicken, despite a tasty sauce, was extremely dry. The rice was offensive. It had clearly been sitting in the rice cooker for some time, long enough to form a skin/shell. Give your rice a fluff, you monsters!

title: Nada Bakery
excerpt:
Steak, confit garlic, and parmesan pie
Pumpkin and bacon quiche
Apple danish
Carrot cake

Nada Bakery is a pretty popular place, especially for a rainy Sunday lunchtime. They were doing a steady trade in both dine-in and takeaway. We can see why. The cabinet had plenty of options and almost everything looked good. Their walls were covered in pie-related accolades, and having sampled their wares these seem deserved. The pie was quite special, although the pastry top was slightly over done.

The quiche was nothing special. This happens sometimes with quiches, where all you can taste is a little bit of bacon, while the pumpkin is visible but not tasteable. Is it that they haven’t roasted the pumpkin? Perhaps it just needed the addition of something else to help the pumpkin sing? A relish certainly wouldn’t have gone astray.

Danishes are one of God’s special tasty treats, and this one didn’t disappoint. Unconventionally they also offered a pineapple Danish, which we don’t think we’ve ever seen before. The carrot cake was trying hard, and they’d made real effort to jam pack it with nuts and fruit. They’d even gone to the effort to split it in 3 and ice between the layers. Unfortunately, this was their downfall. The icing was incredibly sweet, sickly even. We had assumed it was a cream cheese icing based on the look, but to taste there was little, or perhaps no cream cheese actually present. Unfortunately all the sugar ruined the whole thing and left you with that cloying quality on the back of your palate where you were just searching for water.

Speaking of, we saw that one other dine-in table had a bottle of water, but heaven knows where they got that. The ambiance wasn’t great - this place is definitely more of a bakery than a cafe. And half of the Fee-Rex’s chair was covered in dirt like it had been stacked up outside. But despite a few issues, we’d be very happy to try more of what Nada Bakery has to offer.

title: 1154 Pastaria
excerpt:
Gnocchi with a creamy mushroom sauce and spinach
Spinach and ricotta ravioli with a brown butter sauce
Garlic and rosemary roll

It confuses and perplexes us that we don’t see more pasta out there. Everyone loves pasta, it’s easy (relatively) to make, and it’s generally affordable. Maybe this is why 1154 is pumping every single time we walk past. But caution to those who don’t like communal dining experiences, this is a big-table-sit-with-other-people type of situation. This also means there’s no bookings, you just walk in, which suits us to the ground, but perhaps isn’t your cup of tea.

You could tell the pasta was homemade, and we have to give props to the gnocchi. The Fee-Rex isn’t a big gnocchi head, probably because so many of them are terrible, but these were little pillows of heaven. The sauce was also fantastic, the nuts added a great crunch and the mushroom bits were just the right size. Business Andy found the dish a little wearing over time, but perhaps that was because it started from such a lofty height.

The ravioli was also good. Both the raviolis themselves and the whole dish were generously sized. A little gripe about the bread. It was great for dipping into your pasta sauce, and it was affordable too. But it is not to be eaten alone, and if you don’t have bread then you will find yourself with too much leftover sauce. We recommend purchasing one bread each and dipping, but don’t bother eating it by itself.

The ravioli was also good. Both the raviolis themselves and the whole dish were generously sized. A little gripe about the bread. It was great for dipping into your pasta sauce, and it was affordable too. But it is not to be eaten alone, and if you don’t have bread then you will find yourself with too much leftover sauce. We recommend purchasing one bread each and dipping, but don’t bother eating it by itself.

title: Thai Panda
excerpt:
Massaman curry with slow cooked beef
Beef pad Thai

Thai Panda is a Chinese-Thai restaurant on the town edge of Picton. At 7:15 on a Friday night, nobody was there. This didn’t help the ambiance, which was already a bit grim. Restaurants in converted villas can come across homely and warm, or they can come across sad and cheap. This was the latter. The decor was very Facebook Marketplace. Every table was different, with different chairs, like they’d just grabbed whatever was going for $35 or less. Ours was a circular glass topped outdoor table. They did at least have the heat pump cranking.

The menu was much more Thai than Panda, to the point that you wonder why they were bothering with the Chinese at all. But who knows, maybe we missed a trick by going for two Thai staples instead of sampling their very small Chinese menu. It’s highly likely that we’ll never know.

The massaman curry was only okay, the Fee-Rex quite enjoyed the curry sauce, although Business Andy wasn’t on board. We were startled to discover that there were several pieces of pineapple trying to pass themselves off as potato mixed in, and frankly, we have questions. What on earth was that about? Was there a Picton-wide shortage of potato? Surely you wouldn’t choose to diverge from the traditional ingredients list just for the sake of pineapple, isn’t it more expensive than potato? Who wants that anyway? We did both appreciate that the meat was definitely slow cooked and (mostly) just fell apart. We didn’t appreciate the blubbery gristly bits that we found on far too many pieces of meat, however, they really pulled this dish down in our esteem. The non-slow-cooked beef in the pad Thai was definitely of a different ilk, but it just wasn’t good. Maybe we made a mistake by going for a slightly off centre pick for meat in a pad Thai, but if it’s going to be that bad, then just don’t offer it. But that was far from the only issue with the pad Thai, the entire dish was suffused with a flavour that we can only describe as bafflingly lacking. Perhaps the same madness that gripped the chef when they poured an entire tin of pineapple pieces into the massaman curry gripped them again when they were preparing the pad Thai, and they just didn’t put in any of the traditional delicious whatever it is that normally goes into a pad Thai. Either way, avoid.

Sometimes when we come out of a 1, we’re upset, mad even. But not tonight. This time we were overcome by a powerful sadness. This place may have been someone’s dream once, but it’s not looking good. Thai Panda is slightly off the beaten path, and the impression you get from the street is hardly welcoming, this is probably why they are completely empty on a Friday night. And that’s not to say it’s all bad, in fact they are doing some things really well, the service was excellent and our meals came out almost comically fast. But the overall dining experience sadly fell short of even the meh category, and we can only give them our lowest score.

title: Havana Bar
excerpt:
Croquettes with jamón, béchamel, and parmesan
Sourdough with salted butter
Roast squash with orange mascarpone and pomegranate seeds
Beef brisket burger with fries
Fried chicken with cilantro sour cream

Havana Bar, Havana Bar, Havana Bar. I wish we could say we were surprised or disappointed to see you fall out of the fours and down to the threes. But the truth is that your record is spotty, you’ve yo-yo’d three to four on each of the 4 occasions we’ve dined with you.

Case in point, this dinner. We weren’t upset to eat it, in fact it was really nice, it just wasn’t great, and the cocktails that normally pull you up were bringing you down. It started really strong with an excellent sourdough, and then an even more excellent roast squash dish. But then came the too béchamel forward croquettes, which ended up just a bit too one-note. Likewise, the chicken lacked interest. It was a bit dry, and all you really got was a pile of paprika. The worst was the overly dry burger, somehow they’d managed to dry out their beef brisket.

Hopefully next time we visit Havana Bar, they will yo-yo back up to a 4. Time will tell.

title: Aries Restaurant
excerpt:
Sweet pork pastries
Spring rolls
BBQ pork buns
Fried pork dumplings
Soupy pork dumplings
Sweet coconut breads

We hadn’t expected to run into Yum Cha, but we should have. It’s a classic Sunday lunch, and we’re in the business of eating lunch on Sundays, so that’s on us for not putting 2 and 2 together. But it was with some trepidation that we approached Aries Restaurant, it’s been well over a decade since either of us has had Yum Cha, and we don’t remember it fondly.

This place was absolutely heaving with people, and they were revelling in it. The staff were all super friendly, and the service was uniformly great, the food was more miss than hit, however. We liked the soupy dumplings and the sweet coconut bread. We hated the sweet pork pastries. Everything else was just okay.

Bookings recommended (for Yum Cha anyway).

title: Highwater Eatery
excerpt:
Chef’s menu

Congratulations, Highwater Eatery, it’s a pretty big deal to be a four. We award them quite rarely. And it’s really satisfying to go and independently give a four to somewhere that perhaps feels a bit hard done by to not catch a Michelin star recently. Does this mean that actually we’re better reviewers than the fat tire man? We’ll leave the answer of that question up to you.

We’ve said this before, but we’ll say it again. The mark of a great dish is serving you something that you think you don’t like, and showing you how it can be delicious. Neither of us likes mussels, but the mussel emulsion that came with the karaage chicken was outstanding. And that’s not to say that the chicken itself wasn’t incredible too, because it was, but this whole dish came together to become something greater than the sum of its parts. This was the stand out dish of the night, and the field was competitive. We only sampled part of the menu, but there were no fails, and there was plenty more on the menu that sounded similarly good.

And without gushing too much, the dessert was fantastic too. It was a cold apple crumble. If you thought this ws just an apple crumble that was served room temperature, as we did, you’d be wrong. It had been transformed into a whipped, cold sensation that was vanilla-y and delicious. We were entranced.

We could wax lyrical about this meal for a while, but we’ll distill it down. Yum yum yum, try Highwater.

Bookings recommended.

P.S. Extra special shout out to the dude who stuffed his nose into the bucket of cutlery and gave it a giant whiff while we were watching. We still don’t know what this was about, but we have speculated for hours and can only assume it was related to quality control somehow.

title: The Botanist
excerpt:
Breakfast halloumi bao bun
Tofu bao bun
Deep fried cauliflower

This is our third time dining at The Botanist, and our third time complaining about their service. In fairness, the service was better than the previous outings, but there was a service incident which can not go un-discussed. Get a load of this.

We ordered two cocktails with our meal, one espresso martini and one paloma. When the cocktails arrived however, it was two espresso martinis. Easy mistake, no problem. We let them know, and they took one of the drinks away. We could hear them up at the bar saying that there was a mistake, and this espresso martini was meant to be a paloma. We were confident that the paloma would appear momentarily. Then we waited. And waited. The food came. We ate half the food. Then finally the paloma showed up. This is already not great, but what we are about to share with you rocked us to our core. The table next to us was also drinking espresso martinis. The waitress who had removed our mistake-tini took it from the bar to our neighbouring table. And then, within clear ear- and eye-shot of us, said to them “hey do you guys want this espresso martini, it was made by mistake and I’d hate to see it go to waste.” EXCUSE ME? Aren’t we the ones who had the inconvenience of the drink order mistake, and subsequently waited three lifetimes for the correct drink to arrive?? Why would you offer the free drink to some random table, and not to us??? Are these table some kind of VIPs???? Are you worried about “rewarding” us, perhaps suspicious we actually did order two espresso martinis then changed our minds????? Shocking.

Luckily for The Botanist, they make an incredible plate of fried cauliflower. We loved it in 2022, and it stands up gloriously on repeat dining. We eat a lot of fried cauliflower but this was definitely a cut above the rest. The florets were large and meaty, gloriously crisp, so hot, not greasy, a great dipping sauce, and cooked to absolute perfection being neither too hard nor too soft. The bigger the florets, the harder it is to achieve this, so we were very impressed.

The bao buns were acceptable. Their biggest issue was structure, both of them being stacked in a way that made it hard to eat with your hands. So we used knives and forks, but then you’re dealing with issues of mouthful composition. The flavour was a bit same-y between the two, but we appreciated the inventiveness of the breakfast bao offering.

title: 1852 Pub & Kitchen
excerpt:
Cheese pizza
Beef & caramelised onion pizza

“1841 was the year which this great community of ours was settled by Frank Johnson. 1841 Bar and Restaurant is here to bring good old fashioned local hospitality to Johnsonville and the wider Wellington Community.”

Oh, sorry, wrong pub.

“1852 was the year which this great community of ours was settled by John Fitchett. 1852 Pub and Kitchen is here to bring good old fashioned local hospitality to Brooklyn and the wider Wellington Community.”

Did you think we wouldn’t work this out? Upon seeing 1852, we immediately thought it was a sister of that-pub-in-Johnsonville-with-numbers-for-a-name. But then, upon some Googling, there was no apparent link. It wasn’t until we were in the belly of the beast and reading about their copy pasted proud heritage, and browsing their familiar menu, that we made the link. While we could find no actual documentation that these restaurants are the same, they definitely are.

1841 was awarded a 1 in 2024. Normally, a 1 doesn’t get a second chance. Tonight, through deception, they did. And they have risen to the heights of a 2. Admittedly this is a big improvement, but then it would be nigh on impossible to be worse.

We love a bargain. We had initially planned to order one pizza and some nachos, but upon hearing that it was 2-for-1 pizza night, our hands were tied. On the plus side, the pizzas were piping hot with an alright base, and the meat on the pizza was of good quality, no gristly steak here. However, the distribution of pizza sauce was uneven, with some areas of the cheese pizza getting way more than their share. Business Andy had a couple of bites of camembert that he was highly offended by, in fact he used the word ‘ghastly’.

Perhaps they will try to get a third go around, to bring themselves up to a 3. We are on high alert for 1863 lurking for us in another suburb.

title: Simmer Cafe
excerpt:
Roast vegetable salad
Pumpkin soup
Coffee eclair

At 1 on a Saturday afternoon, Simmer Cafe was pumping. There was one available table, still with the previous diners’ dishes on it, and we had to lunge to it to mercilessly outcompete another couple. But as we have experienced on multiple occasions, popularity does not necessarily correlate with quality.

Let’s start with the positive. The pumpkin soup was fantastic. Really flavourful, seeds on top for texture, beautiful bread, ample butter, and a fair price to boot.

We love roast veggie salad, and it continues to baffle us how so many eateries get this simple dish very wrong. Simmer had ballsed up the veggie selection. Yes, there were some roast veg - carrot, pumpkin, red onion, red capsicum, maybe some kumara. But about half the veg was not roast - mushroom, broccoli, celery, some stringy green thing we’re not even sure what it was. What were these doing in here? Is this a ‘chef’s salad’ situation, where you’re just throwing whatever veggies you have lying around in to use them up? The selection came across as thoughtless. Worse still, they’d drowned it in a honey mustard dressing, then to top it off had poorly heated it so while some was warm, some was definitely not.

The coffee eclair was a disappointment. Call us crazy, but when we order a coffee flavoured pastry, we expect it to taste at least a little like coffee. This was sweet, and had a nicely textured inner cream and top icing, but coffee it certainly was not.

Bookings recommended.

title: The Original Thai Restaurant
excerpt:
Peanut satay chicken
Thick red curry beef
Roti
Rice

It can be quite intimidating when you realise that you’ve walked into a local fixture unprepared, unknowing, wide-eyed and not expecting to see multiple hugs handed out, several different instances of plans made between customer and proprietor, and promises to return left, right, and centre.

But you also love to see it, it’s like watching wild animals who don’t know that David Attenborough is just over there filming them. You get to see the native Island Bayers in their habitat, free, just living their best lives. Their best lives are at The Original Thai Restaurant and they have been since 1993. Unreal, what longevity. We wondered how they had done it, until we saw the owner just straight vibing with every single patron. We’ve never even noticed this place befoire, but we felt special and valued.

They have a dark secret, however. There’s a minimum charge per person, a minimum charge that is just above the price of almost every dish on the menu. They have upsold almost every single person who walked in the door. But the owner is so friendly, so funny, so energetic, that you leave feeling like it was worth it anyway just to see him do the monkey dance and crack jokes all night.

The food was only okay. Despite winning a Dominion Post award for great value in the year 2000, things have slipped in the intervening 26 years. When the meals came, we thought they were actually pretty small. This, and the $30 minimum charge, were why basically everybody except us ordered both entree and main.

We appreciated being served rice Mum-style from the big silver pot, it gave a lovely friendly vibe. But the flavours were so-so, there was unwelcome surprise pineapple in the chicken dish, and The Fee-Rex got some gristle to boot.

Bookings recommended.

We appreciated being served rice Mum-style from the big silver pot, it gave a lovely friendly vibe. But the flavours were so-so, there was unwelcome surprise pineapple in the chicken dish, and The Fee-Rex got some gristle to boot.

Bookings recommended.

title: The Realm Hataitai
excerpt:
Chicken burger
Margherita pizza

There is an unspoken rule in hospitality around warning customers about wait times. Some may even call it a duty. An imperative. A mandate. When we walked in and saw two large tables and the rest of the restaurant empty, we weren’t concerned. We saw they had some food and figured we were in the clear. This was reinforced by the waitress saying flat zero about any extended waits.

When we saw more food coming out of the kitchen we thought ooh, this could be for us. But wait, that’s two pizzas. Going to the other table. Then a break. Then two more pizzas. Then a break. And so forth.

Over forty-five minutes we waited. And yes, the blow was softened by their reasonably priced cocktails. But nonetheless, a dereliction of duty has occurred here. Not everybody has 45+ minutes up their sleeve on a Saturday afternoon. At one point, well into the wait, the server said “yours is out next”. It wasn’t. And it wasn’t the food  after that either. Did she mean yours is the next table? That’s bloody cheeky phrasing when there’s only three tables here and two have 10+ people.

When the food finally did arrive, one was worth the wait and one wasn’t. The burger was joyful. Structural integrity on point, you could put this thing down and pick it up to your hearts content. The perfect level of spice, crispy hot chicken, just the right amount of salad, and the pickled onion was a nice touch. The margherita pizza wasn’t bad, but it was floppy, over-cheesed, and the crust was chewy.

title: Afghan Darbar Restaurant & Takeaway
excerpt:
Banjan boranee
Karahi lamb

We dined at Afghan Darbar early in our relationship, before we were keeping BAATFR records. We do not remember it fondly. So when the gods of randomisation brought Afghan Darbar to us again tonight, our emotions were mixed. On one hand, we were quite pleased to see they were still going. Afghani is not a well-represented cuisine in NZ, so we liked that there was support for something different. On the other hand, we were nervous to return to a previous unpleasant dining experience.

Interestingly, the components of the dishes that The Fee-Rex found most pleasant, Business Andy found least pleasant, and vice versa. The Fee-Rex disliked that lamb the most, and found the eggplant kind of indeterminate and smooshy, while Business Andy disliked the mint sauce that was all over the salad, and unfortunately experienced some very thin naan bread.

What we do agree on is that the general ambiance was quite lacking. It was cold for a start, not quite leave-the-doors-wide-open-in-August cold, (looking at you Kaimak Johnsonville), but still cold. The chairs were uncomfortable, and it was awkwardly quiet, so we spent the entire meal listening in to our fellow diners and speculating wildly about their lives.

title: East Pier Hotel
excerpt:
Bread with dips
Korean chicken
Fried halloumi
Basque cheesecake

East Pier is a sizeable restaurant, the kind of place where they can easily close off a couple of rooms for private events, and is located right on the Ahuriri waterfront. Their prices reflect this. $27 for a mediocre cocktail? $25 for five small pieces of fried chicken? The prices, and the quality, are reflective of a we’re-in-a-plum-spot-and-people-will-come-here-no-matter-what attitude. Admittedly, sitting in the Napier sun on a still August’s day was nice, and the first real sunshine we’ve seen in months (thanks, Wellington). And the food wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t anything you’d make a fuss over. Even trying to think of which dishes were best, or worst, feels a bit redundant, it was all just a forgettable pile of average. Actually, no. We thought that the little coleslaw was a good accompaniment to the halloumi, cutting through the greasiness. The lettuce leaves served with the chicken were a less successful version of the same concept.

title: Highway 57 Bakery & Cafe
excerpt:
Butter chicken pie
Tandoori chicken croissant
Apricot almond tartlet
Banana smoothie

When is a banana smoothie not a banana smoothie? When it’s a banana milkshake. We’ve said it before, but clearly it bears repeating - if there is no real banana in your smoothie, it is a milkshake. Today’s beverage was cold, sweet, banana-ey, by all accounts a decent banana milkshake, but a smoothie it was not, no Sir. And they have been penalised accordingly. But this was hardly their only foible.

The pie innards were genuinely boring. Perhaps this is what the everyman wants from a butter chicken pie, but it could at least afford to taste like something. Anything. This was a real shame because the pie crust was sensational, light, flaky, just fantastic. There’s a chance that another pie out of this cabinet could have dragged their overall score up, kicking and screaming, into the good side of average.

The croissant was overall forgettable, they had absolutely squashed it flat to toast it, which made it look a bit funny, but that was the most notable thing about it. And the tartlet was inoffensive but dull. We also look sceptically at any establishment that insists on glad wrapping every single item in their cabinet individually. You just can’t help but wonder how long they have been sitting there when they are all wrapped for maximum freshness and longevity.
